lines.say: In 1990, Poland's entire economy was worth 66 billion US dollars. That was about a quarter of Sweden's.
In 2025, it crossed one trillion dollars. And it's now just nine billion short of Switzerland.
Poland is just one of the stories in fifty-five years of Europe's economic race. Let's watch it happen.

card: GDP: the value of everything a country produces in a year
lines.say: First, what the bars show. Each one is a country's GDP: the value of everything it produces in a year.

card: At each year's prices and exchange rates. Source: World Bank
lines.say: It's in US dollars, at each year's prices and exchange rates, and every figure comes from the World Bank.

card: The big EU members, the UK, Switzerland and Norway
lines.say: We've included fourteen of Europe's largest economies: the big EU members, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and Norway.

card: Russia and Turkey: largely outside Europe, and no World Bank figures for Russia before 1989
lines.say: Russia and Turkey aren't in this race. A large part of each lies outside Europe, and the World Bank's figures for Russia only start in 1989.

card: A World Bank estimate for today's Germany, worked back from West Germany's growth
lines.say: One note on Germany. Before 1991, the World Bank estimates the whole of today's Germany by working backwards from West Germany's growth.

card: A bar can jump or drop when a currency moves, even if nothing changed at home
lines.say: And because everything is in dollars, a bar can jump or drop when a currency moves, even if nothing changed at home. Keep that in mind. It explains several of the twists ahead.
1970. Germany leads, with 217 billion dollars. Then France, the United Kingdom and Italy.

lines.note: Poland: World Bank figures start in 1990
lines.say: Spain is fifth, at 41 billion, a long way behind. Ireland is last, at just four billion. And Poland isn't here yet: the World Bank's figures for it start in 1990.
Through the 1970s, every bar grows fast. Some of that is real growth, but much of it is inflation and a weakening dollar.
By 1980, Germany has passed 950 billion dollars.
Then something strange happens. Between 1980 and 1985, almost every bar shrinks. Spain falls from 233 billion dollars to 181.
Europe didn't get poorer. The dollar became very strong, so each country's output was worth fewer dollars. It's the clearest example on this chart of a currency moving the bars.
Now watch Italy and the United Kingdom. In 1986, Italy moves ahead of Britain.

lines.note: 1986 · Il sorpasso: Italy passes the UK
lines.say: Italians called it il sorpasso, the overtaking, and it was celebrated in Rome.
Britain takes the place back in 1988, then loses it again a year later.

lines.note: 1990 · Poland enters at $66 bn · Ireland $49 bn
lines.say: 1990. Germany is reunited. And a new name appears near the bottom of the chart: Poland, at 66 billion dollars, thirteenth of our fourteen. Ireland is even smaller, at 49 billion.
Britain finally settles ahead of Italy for good in 1994. Both economies were growing. The swaps mostly follow the exchange rate between the lira and the pound.
In 1997, the UK passes France for second place, helped by a strong pound. Germany stays first, as it will in every single year on this chart.
The euro arrives in 1999, and for its first few years it's weak against the dollar. That holds the eurozone's bars back.

lines.note: 2007 · Germany $3.48 tn · UK $3.11 tn · France $2.66 tn
lines.say: Then it strengthens, and by 2007, Europe's bars are higher than ever. Germany, three and a half trillion dollars. The UK, three point one. France, two point seven.
Spain has been booming. By 2008, its economy is worth one point six trillion dollars: almost forty times its size in 1970.
Then the financial crisis. The pound falls hard, and in 2009 France takes second place back from the UK.
Spain's housing bubble bursts, and its economy shrinks for years.
Second place changes hands again in 2012, 2013 and 2014: three swaps in three years. Since 2014, the UK has kept second place in dollar terms.
2015. The euro falls sharply against the dollar. Add up all fourteen economies, and they shrink by about twelve percent in a single year, from 18.3 trillion dollars to 16.2.

Now look at Ireland. In 2015, its official growth was so large that economists nicknamed it leprechaun economics. Big international companies had moved valuable assets, and the profits that come with them, to Ireland.
That's why Ireland's own government uses a different measure, called modified national income, when it plans its budget. On this chart, Ireland looks richer than it feels on the ground.

lines.note: 2022 · Oil and gas prices lift Norway to 9th
lines.say: 2022. The dollar is strong again, and most bars dip. But not Norway's. With oil and gas prices soaring, Norway jumps to ninth place.

lines.note: Energy prices fall back, and so does Norway
lines.say: When energy prices fall back, so does Norway. By 2025, it's down to thirteenth.
And Poland. Through the 2000s and 2010s, it trades places with Belgium, Sweden and Norway again and again. From 2018, it stays ahead of all three.

In 2025, Poland crosses one trillion dollars: 1.035 trillion. Switzerland is at 1.044 trillion. A year earlier, the gap was 52 billion. Now it's nine. If 2026 looks anything like 2025, Poland passes Switzerland next year.

So here is 2025. Germany: 5.05 trillion dollars, first in every year since 1970. The UK, 4.0 trillion. France, 3.37. Italy, 2.55. Spain, 1.91. The Netherlands, 1.33. Then Switzerland and Poland, almost touching.

take: Germany, the UK, France and Italy, in some order, for 55 years
lines.say: Three things to take away. One: the top four haven't changed in fifty-five years. Germany, the UK, France and Italy, in some order.

take: Exchange rates, not sudden riches, explain most changes at the top
lines.say: Two: most of the swaps between them come from exchange rates, not from one country suddenly getting rich.

take: The real movers started far behind
Spain: about 46 times its 1970 size. Poland: more than 15 times its 1990 size
lines.say: Three: the real movers started far behind. In dollar terms, Spain's economy is about forty-six times bigger than in 1970, and Poland's is more than fifteen times bigger than in 1990.
But dollars per country don't tell you how well people live. Next on Terrachart: minimum wages in every EU country, and what they really buy. And after that, how Poland caught up.
Sources are in the description. If you think we should have measured this differently, tell us in the comments. We read them.
